Glossary

    Power, root, logarithm

    Words: 1984

    A power and the two questions that invert it. At school the root and the logarithm are studied in different years, in different chapters and with different rules. In fact they are two questions to one equality, and their laws are one law of powers read from different sides.

    Main idea of the page #

    The equality an=ba^n = b has three participants. An unknown bb is a power, an unknown aa is a root, an unknown nn is a logarithm. So the properties of logarithms need not be learnt separately: they are the properties of powers written for the exponent. Their restrictions are shared too: they come from the fact that a positive number stays positive in any power.

    Step 0 · Hook

    1 · What the root of x² equals #

    Simplify x2\sqrt{x^2}. The usual answer: «the root and the square cancel each other, so xx».

    Let us check with a number. Let x=−3x = -3. Then (−3)2=9=3\sqrt{(-3)^2} = \sqrt{9} = 3, not −3. The root of the square returned not the number but its distance to zero:

    x2=|x|\sqrt{x^2} = |x|

    The second hook: what is log2(−8)\log_2(-8)? The question reads: «to what power must 2 be raised to get −8?». There is no such power: two to any power is positive. Both hooks have one source, and below it will become visible.

    Step 1 · Concept

    2 · One equality, three questions #

    A PowerThe product of n equal factors a; fractional and negative exponents extend this definition.To the glossary with a natural exponent is a product of equal factors: an=a·a·…·aa^n = a \cdot a \cdot \ldots \cdot a (nn factors). Take the equality 23=82^3 = 8 and ask about each participant:

    • the base 2 and the exponent 3 are known, we seek the result - this is a power: 23=82^3 = 8;
    • the exponent 3 and the result 8 are known, we seek the base - this is a n-th rootThe number that gives b when raised to the power n.To the glossary : 83=2\sqrt[3]{8} = 2;
    • the base 2 and the result 8 are known, we seek the exponent - this is a LogarithmThe exponent to which the base a must be raised to get b.To the glossary : log28=3\log_2 8 = 3.

    Figure 22. One equality, three questions: power, root, logarithm.

    Hence two definitions worth reading as questions:

    • bn\sqrt[n]{b} is the number that gives bb in the power nn;
    • logab\log_a b is the exponent to which aa must be raised to get bb.
    Step 2 · Law

    3 · One law in three notations #

    Law of powers: multiplying powers adds exponents

    am·an=am+na^m \cdot a^n = a^{m+n}

    The same law read for the exponent

    loga(xy)=logax+logay\log_a (xy) = \log_a x + \log_a y

    The definition of the logarithm in one line

    alogab=ba^{\log_a b} = b

    Root of a square

    a2=|a|\sqrt{a^2} = |a|

    The other properties are consequences of these four: a quotient of powers gives a difference of exponents and the logarithm of a quotient, a power of a power gives a product of exponents and the rule logaxk=klogax\log_a x^k = k \log_a x.

    Step 3 · Why it is so

    4 · Where the law comes from and why it was invented #

    Power. ama^m has mm factors, ana^n has another nn. Together there are m+nm + n of them. No more proof is needed.

    Logarithm. Let x=amx = a^m and y=any = a^n, that is, m=logaxm = \log_a x, n=logayn = \log_a y. By the law of powers xy=am+nxy = a^{m+n}, so the exponent of the product equals m+nm + n. That is exactly loga(xy)=logax+logay\log_a(xy) = \log_a x + \log_a y.

    Why. Logarithms appeared in 1614 with John Napier precisely for the sake of this law: multiplying large numbers was replaced by adding their logarithms from a table. A logarithm turns multiplication into addition. This is not a school exercise but a tool with which astronomers computed orbits for more than three centuries, until calculators appeared.

    Root of a square. An Arithmetic rootThe non-negative number whose square equals a given non-negative number.To the glossary is a non-negative number by definition. The squares of the numbers aa and −a-a are the same, and of these two candidates the root picks the non-negative one. That is |a||a|.

    Step 4 · Limits

    5 · Where the laws break #

    The logarithm logab\log_a b exists only for a>0a > 0, a≠1a \neq 1, b>0b > 0. Each condition is not a rule from a textbook but an answer to the question «to what power». A positive base in any power gives a positive number, hence b>0b > 0. One in any power gives 1, so the question «to what power must 1 be raised to get 5» has no answer, while «to get 1» has infinitely many. These three conditions are the domain of every task with a logarithm.

    Figure 23. The logarithm mirrors the power: 2ˣ > 0 always, so log₂ x exists only for x > 0.

    The law loga(xy)=logax+logay\log_a(xy) = \log_a x + \log_a y requires x>0x > 0 and y>0y > 0. The left side exists for two negative factors too: log2((−2)(−4))=log28=3\log_2((-2)(-4)) = \log_2 8 = 3, but the right side does not. So transforming an expression with a logarithm can narrow the domain and lose a root. The honest record: logax2=2loga|x|\log_a x^2 = 2\log_a |x|.

    a2=|a|\sqrt{a^2} = |a|, but (a)2=a(\sqrt{a})^2 = a only for a≥0a \geq 0. An even root of a negative number does not exist among the real numbers, while an odd one does: −83=−2\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2.

    Figure 24. √(x²) = |x|: to the left of zero the root of the square is not x.

    With a base between 0 and 1 the sign of an inequality changes. The functions axa^x and logax\log_a x increase for a>1a > 1 and decrease for 0<a<10 < a < 1. So 0.5x>0.530.5^x > 0.5^3 gives x<3x < 3, not x>3x > 3.

    Step 5 · Practice

    6 · Tasks in the NMT format #

    One answer out of five · 1 point

    Calculate log354−log32\log_3 54 - \log_3 2.

    Law: the logarithm of a product, read for a quotient.

    log354−log32=log3542=log327=3\log_3 54 - \log_3 2 = \log_3 \frac{54}{2} = \log_3 27 = 3. Blind moves: 27 - found the quotient and forgot the logarithm, 52 - subtracted the arguments.

    Short answer · 2 points

    Calculate (1−2)2−2\sqrt{(1 - \sqrt{2})^2} - \sqrt{2}.

    Law: root of a square.

    The number 1−21 - \sqrt{2} is negative, so (1−2)2=|1−2|=2−1\sqrt{(1 - \sqrt{2})^2} = |1 - \sqrt{2}| = \sqrt{2} - 1. In all: 2−1−2=−1\sqrt{2} - 1 - \sqrt{2} = -1. The blind move «the root and the square cancel» gives 1−221 - 2\sqrt{2}, and such an answer cannot even be written in the short form.

    Matching · 3 points

    Match each expression (1-3) with the one equal to it (A-E).

    A · 222^2   B · 282^8   C · 2152^{15}   D · 484^8   E · 2532^{53}

    Law: the law of powers and two of its consequences.

    Multiplication adds the exponents (8), a power of a power multiplies them (15), division subtracts (2). Traps: 484^8 - the bases were multiplied, 2532^{53} - the exponents were «glued».

    One answer out of five · 1 point

    The graph of the function y = log₂ x passes through a point with ordinate 3. Find the abscissa of this point.

    Figure 25. For the task: the point of the logarithm graph with ordinate 3.

    Law: definition of the logarithm.

    log₂ x = 3 means 2³ = x, that is, x = 8. 6 is 2 · 3, 9 is 3², 1.5 is 3 : 2.
    Step 6 · Reverse move

    7 · Name the law yourself #

    The law is not given. First name the laws and the domain, then calculate. The solution opens after you answer.

    Short answer · 2 points

    Solve the equation x+1·log2(x−2)=0\sqrt{x + 1} \cdot \log_2(x - 2) = 0. If there are several roots, write their sum.

    Laws: the domain of the logarithm and the zero product of block 1.

    Domain: x+1≥0x + 1 \geq 0 and x−2>0x - 2 > 0, that is, x>2x > 2. A product equals zero when one of the factors equals zero and both make sense. The first factor gives x=−1x = -1, but there log2(−3)\log_2(-3) does not exist. The second gives x=3x = 3. Answer: 3. The blind move without the domain gives two roots and the sum 2. An equation of this type (a product of an irrational and a logarithmic expression) was among the hardest tasks of NMT 2026.

    Short answer · 2 points

    Calculate 5log57+15^{\log_5 7 + 1}.

    Laws: the law of powers and the definition of the logarithm.

    5log57+1=5log57·51=7·5=355^{\log_5 7 + 1} = 5^{\log_5 7} \cdot 5^1 = 7 \cdot 5 = 35. A sum in the exponent is a product of powers: the law of powers read from right to left.

    Short answer · 2 points

    Calculate log23·log34\log_2 3 \cdot \log_3 4.

    Law: change of base, a consequence of the definition of the logarithm.

    log23=1log32\log_2 3 = \frac{1}{\log_3 2}, so the product equals log34log32=log24=2\frac{\log_3 4}{\log_3 2} = \log_2 4 = 2. The chain «from 2 to 3, from 3 to 4» gives «from 2 to 4».

    8 · Find the mistake in someone else's solution #

    Petro solves the equation log2x2=2\log_2 x^2 = 2: «By the property of the logarithm log2x2=2log2x\log_2 x^2 = 2\log_2 x, so log2x=1\log_2 x = 1 and x=2x = 2. There is one root».

    Where is the mistake?

    The expression log2x2\log_2 x^2 exists for all x≠0x \neq 0, while 2log2x2\log_2 x exists only for x>0x > 0. Petro narrowed the domain and lost the root x=−2x = -2. Correctly: x2=4x^2 = 4, x=±2x = \pm 2, two roots. This is the second limit of the law.

    What you have after this page #

    One law of powers instead of three lists of properties. The properties of roots and logarithms need not be kept in memory separately: they can be derived from am·an=am+na^m \cdot a^n = a^{m+n} in a minute. And the domain of a logarithm is not a rule that is easy to forget but an answer to the question «to what power».

    Frequency on this site, not in the NMT: this page has 7 trainer tasks, and they lean on these laws: The definition of the logarithm in one line - 3, Law of powers: multiplying powers adds exponents - 2, Domain of the logarithm - 1, Root of a square - 1, The same law read for the exponent - 1, Zero product - 1. In real NMT papers of 2024-2026 this block is needed in 26 tasks out of 132: Law of powers: multiplying powers adds exponents - 18, The definition of the logarithm in one line - 10, The same law read for the exponent - 1.

    You know this law if you:

    1. solve 8 tasks out of 10 on powers, roots and logarithms without a hint;
    2. can explain aloud why the logarithm of a product equals the sum of the logarithms;
    3. find the mistake in someone else's solution, as in Petro's.
